name: The Cockspur Hawthorn of Cylburn Arboretum

location.address: Cylburn Arboretum, 4915 Greenspring Ave, Baltimore, MD 21209 (exact spot within the 207-acre grounds not pinned this pass; not one of the 17 specimens on the arboretum's own printed 'Notable Trees' map, so it stands somewhere else on the property)

verified_sources: https://www.baltimoresun.com/2023/11/29/touring-baltimores-big-trees-in-an-oasis-of-beauty-guest-commentary/ (Baltimore Sun guest commentary, 29 Nov 2023, by a named tree tour guide describing a walk through Cylburn Arboretum: calls this tree 'Cylburn's only remaining state champion' and describes it firsthand in late autumn as 'leafless but teeming with berry-like fruit called haws', with 'long sharp thorns that resemble a giant's toothpick' -- a specific, physically checkable eyewitness description, not a copied stat)
access: Free, public city-owned arboretum (Baltimore City Department of Recreation and Parks / Cylburn Arboretum Friends). Open daily except Mondays, no admission charge, per Wikipedia's Cylburn Arboretum article and the arboretum's own trail map.
transport: Northwest Baltimore, accessible by MTA Bus Route #1; parking on site.
verify_notes: SINGLE SOURCE this pass, shipped per Step 2's explicit rule that a single-sourced tree ships flagged rather than being held back. Tried and failed to get a second source or exact location in the time available: (1) Cylburn Arboretum Friends' own official 'Notable Trees' map (cylburn.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/01/cylburn_tree_shrubs_map.pdf), which letter-codes 17 specimens A-Q with approximate positions relative to the Mansion/Visitor Center/Greenhouses, does NOT include this hawthorn -- it lists a Castor Aralia (Kalopanax pictus) as the arboretum's STATE Champion (point O on that map) instead, which conflicts with the Sun's 2023 'only remaining state champion' description of the hawthorn. Read together, the two most likely explanations are that the printed map (undated on its face, hosted since at least 2013) is simply older than 2023 and the Castor Aralia has since died or lost its state-champion status, or that the map was never a complete list of every champion on the grounds. Either way, DO NOT independently repeat the Castor Aralia's 'State Champion' label as current fact without rechecking it (left as a separate lead below). (2) The Maryland Big Tree Program's own database (mdbigtrees.org, 'Tree Listings'/'State Champion Trees') is JS-rendered and would not return tree-level data to this pass's fetch tool; a future pass with a JS-capable fetch or the ability to query its underlying data could likely get exact circumference/height/crown and possibly a precise location, which would let this tree's location_precision move from approximate to confirmed. (3) TreeBaltimore's own notable-trees page mentions an interactive ArcGIS 'Notable Tree Map' for the whole city but the page fetched did not surface a Cylburn/hawthorn entry directly; the ArcGIS web app itself (arcgis.com webappviewer id d2cfbbe9a24b4d988de127852e6c26c8) was not queryable with the tools available this pass. No girth or height figure was found anywhere this pass; the Sun's description is purely visual/seasonal (bare branches, red haws, long thorns), which is itself decent 'alive and observed recently' evidence (Nov 2023) even without measurements. location_precision is approximate at the arboretum's own address/coordinate, honestly short of pinning which part of the 207-acre grounds holds it.
story:
Cylburn Arboretum's cockspur hawthorn carries thorns long enough that a Baltimore Sun guest columnist compared them to a giant's toothpick, straight, sharp and several inches each, the kind farmers once grew into living fences because nothing could push through them. This one grows loose rather than clipped, somewhere in the arboretum's 207 acres on Baltimore's northwest side.

The same columnist, touring the grounds in late 2023, called it Cylburn's only remaining state champion, the last of a run of record trees the arboretum used to hold more of. That claim sits next to a complication: the arboretum's own printed trail map names a different tree, a castor aralia, as the state champion instead. Titles like this move when a tree grows, dies or gets remeasured, and a printed map does not always catch up. Either the aralia has since lost the title or the map is simply the older document.

What the newspaper account gives that the map cannot is a direct look, taken in November: bare branches carrying a heavy load of small red haws, and those thorns.

Nobody has measured its girth or dated it, and this pass could not pin which part of the grounds it stands on. If you find it, the thorns and the fruit are how you will know.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the thorns, several inches long and straight, and by the small red haws that hang on through a leafless November. It stands somewhere in the arboretum grounds; nobody has pinned the exact spot.
why_go: A hawthorn a Baltimore Sun tour guide called Cylburn Arboretum's last remaining state champion, armed with thorns long enough to compare to a giant's toothpick.

name: The Paperbark Maple of Cylburn Arboretum

location.address: Cylburn Arboretum, 4915 Greenspring Ave, Baltimore, MD 21209, near the Visitor Center (marked point 'A' on the arboretum's own printed trail map, close to the parking area and Greenspring Ave entrance)

verified_sources: https://www.baltimoresun.com/2023/11/29/touring-baltimores-big-trees-in-an-oasis-of-beauty-guest-commentary/ (Baltimore Sun guest commentary, 29 Nov 2023: names this a Baltimore City Champion, gives a champion score of 91 points, and describes it firsthand: 'exfoliating and intense cinnamon colored bark')

https://cylburn.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/01/cylburn_tree_shrubs_map.pdf (Cylburn Arboretum Friends' own official 'Notable Trees' map: point A, 'Paperbark Maple, Acer griseum, City Champion', positioned just southeast of the Visitor Center near the Greenspring Ave entrance -- an independent institutional source, not the newspaper, naming and mapping the same tree with the same champion designation)
access: Free, public city-owned arboretum (Baltimore City Department of Recreation and Parks / Cylburn Arboretum Friends). Open daily except Mondays, no admission charge.
transport: Northwest Baltimore, accessible by MTA Bus Route #1; on-site parking near the Visitor Center, a short walk from point A on the arboretum's own map.
verify_notes: Two independent sources agree on species and City Champion status: the Sun's 2023 firsthand description (bark colour, champion score of 91 points -- the American Forests index, trunk circumference in inches + height in feet + 1/4 average crown spread in feet, not a measurement in itself) and Cylburn Arboretum Friends' own trail map, which places it at labelled point A near the Visitor Center. No circumference, height or age figure found directly (the 91-point score cannot be reverse-engineered into any one of those three without the others, so it is not decomposed here to avoid inventing a number). Paperbark maple is a slow-growing, small ornamental species prized for its exfoliating cinnamon-coloured bark, which is the visible, checkable feature both sources independently point to. location_precision is approximate: point A on the arboretum's own map gives a specific corner of the grounds (near the Visitor Center/parking, by the Greenspring Ave entrance) rather than the full 207 acres, which is a real improvement over park-level, but this pass did not get a GPS-grade coordinate, so it is not marked confirmed. A future pass with a JS-capable fetch against the Maryland Big Tree Program's own database (mdbigtrees.org) may be able to get exact measurements and a precise coordinate for this and the hawthorn above.
story:
A paperbark maple sheds its own bark in curls of cinnamon and copper, thin as paper, and it keeps doing that in every season, which is the whole reason anyone plants one where people will walk past it in winter. Cylburn Arboretum's specimen stands a few steps from the Visitor Center, close enough to the Greenspring Avenue entrance that most visits pass within sight of it without meaning to.

The arboretum's own trail map marks the spot as point A and names it a City Champion. A Baltimore Sun guest columnist, touring the grounds in November 2023, gave it a champion score of 91 points and singled out the same feature the map cannot show: bark peeling back in bright, exfoliating strips. An institution and a firsthand account, written months apart, naming the same tree at the same corner of the grounds.

Neither source gives a single number. A champion score is calculated from circumference, height and crown spread together, and pulling one figure back out of the total would mean inventing what nobody measured directly, so this page carries none. Paperbark maple is naturally a slow, small tree, and holding the city title here says more about how rare the species still is in Baltimore than about size.

Go in low winter light, when the bark catches it best.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the bark: thin curls of cinnamon and copper peeling back in every season, not just autumn. It stands a few steps from the Visitor Center, near the Greenspring Avenue entrance.
why_go: Baltimore's champion paperbark maple, its cinnamon bark peeling in curls year round, a short walk from the arboretum entrance.
